paras: The lynching of Richard Long was the hanging of a prisoner by a masked mob from the Main Street bridge at Kokomo, Indiana, shortly after midnight on the night of April 3-4, 1882. Long, who was reported under many other names, had been arrested on a charge of raping a three-year-old girl, and the mob broke down the jail doors after the sheriff refused to give up the keys. Papers across the country carried the story, many dwelling on the prayer, the song and his plea to be hanged 'decent', and within days a correspondent reported a growing belief that he had been innocent.

According to an Indianapolis dispatch of April 2, a man named in early reports as Charles Gileson of Franklin, Indiana, entered the house of Edward Pritchard at Kokomo at about one o'clock that Sunday morning. The dispatch said he chloroformed the family and carried their three-year-old daughter from her crib to an outhouse, and he was charged with raping her, a child the first reports said was not expected to survive.
The sheriff asked the Governor for help, and one wire said the Governor had called out the military, but no later report mentions troops at Kokomo.

Near midnight on April 3, men who had organized in Haskett's Grove, masked or with their coats turned inside out, marched to Ogden & Reed's blacksmith shop for sledge hammers and crowbars and then went on to the jail. The Sentinel counted 'one hundred masked men', while a condensed wire spoke of 'a mob of eight hundred'; the fuller dispatch said seven or eight hundred onlookers at the jail cheered the masked party.

When the sheriff refused to deliver the keys, the mob broke down the doors and reached the cell in twenty-two minutes. By one account W. F. Vail, a minister and others tried to stop them, but the mob and the crowd answered with 'shouts of derision'.

At the bridge a minister, whose name was printed as McCune, McClure, McClune or McClane, offered a prayer and questioned the prisoner. The prisoner admitted stealing a horse, which another wire said he took at Macy, Indiana, and a watch, but he denied the rape. With his hands and legs tied, he stood on a box, sang 'See that my grave is kept green', said he hoped to meet his father and mother in heaven, and gave his name as Richard Long of Franklin. His last request, 'Hang me decent', was granted, and the Sentinel put the hanging at 1 a.m.

A few days later the Owosso Times in Michigan reported that 'the impression is rapidly gaining ground that Long was innocent'. The same item quoted a leading citizen as saying no assault had been committed and said that Dr. Armstrong, who examined the girl after the hanging, believed the dead man innocent. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage.

The story reached the national press first as a pre-lynching warning, under headlines such as the Kennebec Journal's 'A Case in Which Judge Lynch will Probably Have Jurisdiction'. After the hanging, telegraphic briefs from Washington to Sacramento treated the charge as proven, running under heads such as 'Speedy Vengeance', 'A Beast Hanged' and 'A Rape Flend Lyncked in Indiana'. The Washington Evening Critic headlined its version 'Lynch Law Properly Applied', and the Portland Daily Press used his last words, 'Hang Me Decent'. The wire copy gave the prisoner at least a dozen names, from Gileson and Gibson to Jameson, Jermison, Gunson and Johnson, and one Maine paper put the event in Missouri.

The Monmouth Inquirer remarked how 'formal' the proceedings of Judge Lynch had become, and the Sacramento Record-Union built an ironic editorial, 'The Latest Fashions in Lynching', around the prayer and the song, concluding that law 'in that part of Indiana must have fallen into contempt and distrust'. Indiana's own Sentinel called the prisoner both 'the rape fiend' and 'the poor wretch', and printed its correspondent's report that a great many citizens condemned the affair 'in the most severe terms'.
Headlines and wire copy called the prisoner a rapist, but every account of the hanging says he denied the charge, and the Owosso Times later reported doubt that any assault had occurred.

bases: A masked mob broke into the Kokomo jail and hanged a prisoner charged with assaulting a child from the Main Street bridge (A15, A11, A29).

A mob of about a hundred masked men, or eight hundred by another count, broke down the jail doors after the sheriff refused the keys and hanged the prisoner for an alleged rape of a child (A15, A23, A4).

The Indiana State Sentinel's Kokomo special and the Associated Press dispatch from Indianapolis agree on the jail break and the hanging at the bridge (A15, A11, A29). Some of their wording is shared, but a separate correspondent's item confirms the hanging (A24). Only the man's guilt is disputed.

accounts.gist: Later advices said the belief that Long was innocent was gaining ground; a leading citizen denied any assault, and the examining physician believed him innocent.

framing.detail: The Evening Critic headlined its brief 'Lynch Law Properly Applied.'
Briefs ran under 'Speedy Vengeance', 'A Beast Hanged' and 'A Rape Flend Lyncked in Indiana', calling the accused a rapist outright.
The Indianapolis Sentinel headlined 'The Kokomo Rapist' and called him 'the rape fiend', but also 'the poor wretch', called it 'a terrible affair' and reported citizens' condemnation.
The Sacramento Record-Union's editorial 'The Latest Fashions in Lynching' mocked the prayer and song and concluded that law there had 'fallen into contempt and distrust'.
The Owosso Times called the dead man 'the victim of the lawless mob' and reported that 'sober, second thought' was against the lynching.
The Monmouth Inquirer noted how 'formal' Judge Lynch's proceedings had become.
